text: A lost recipe is not the usual reason a man on the run comes home. Omi left his ancestral village once already, taking his grandfather's money and a plan that involved London; he comes back owing the wrong people, and has to keep a version of himself intact in front of relatives who remember the boy. At 140 minutes the film has room for what a tighter comedy would cut — the kitchen, the uncles, the long afternoons in which a lie has to be held up by hand. A courtship runs alongside the search, and the two get in each other's way. What gives the thing its shape is the object at the centre: an inheritance that is not money or land but a set of instructions nobody wrote down, still carrying the family name.

Sixty-eight minutes, a working city, and a cameraman who keeps turning up inside the picture he is taking. Dziga Vertov filed it as documentary, though little in it behaves like reporting. There is no story to carry the running time, so the organisation has to come from somewhere else — from rhythm, from juxtaposition, from the decision about which two shots sit next to each other. Traffic, machines, crowds and faces are handled as material rather than as events. Both Sight & Sound polls have carried it, the critics' and the directors'. It also sits on a list of the hundred best films in the history of Ukrainian cinema, which is worth knowing: a 1929 Soviet credit covers a great deal of ground, and one part of that ground has kept its claim.

George comes out of prison to find that the sort of hard man he used to be has gone out of date. What is left for him is work as a driver, which puts a small-time criminal in a car with a woman whose clients are well above his station and whose errands he does not fully understand. Neil Jordan builds the film out of that gap in class and knowledge: George reads the city the way he learned to read it years ago, and the city has moved. The search she asks him to make, for a young woman she knew in the King's Cross years, keeps pulling the story down into places the romance cannot follow. It sits in the BFI's hundred British films, and the reason is not the crime plot; it is the driving, and the talk in the car.

Everything in this house gets settled by talk, and the talk is fast, funny and never quite safe. Raymond puts his wife's brother out for using; Val, her mother and her grandmother stay where they are, in a corner of working-class London the film has no intention of leaving. Across two hours and eight minutes the violence registers less as an event that arrives than as a temperature the rooms already hold. Gary Oldman directs without offering the relief of a plot to be solved, which leaves the ordinary intervals — a joke, a round of drinks, an apology — to carry the picture, and those are the hardest stretches to sit through. Nothing is arranged to make the family legible from outside. The difference between a joke and a warning is audible, or it is not.

They meet across a line neither of them names out loud: Sarah works in community health, Joe is the sort of man her work exists for. He is out of a job and off drink, and both conditions are recent enough to still be daily. Ken Loach sets this in one of the harder neighbourhoods of Glasgow and lets the relationship move at the speed such a thing actually moves, which is slowly, with interruptions from other people's emergencies. What is at stake is not whether they like each other. It is whether a man who has organised his whole life around not drinking can also take on the obligations that come with caring about someone living inside the same pressures he does. Speech carries almost everything; an accent and a pause do the work a score would do elsewhere.

A real guitar is the one thing the film's ten-year-old does not have. Dhunu lives in a village in northeast India with her widowed mother, runs with a gang of boys, and wants a band of her own; the wanting is treated as a practical problem rather than a charming one. Rima Das shot it in Assamese at eighty-seven minutes, short enough that nothing gets a second pass, and it came away with the National Film Award for Best Feature Film and the one for editing before going forward as an international submission to the Academy Awards. What holds it together is that Dhunu is never written as an exception to where she lives. The girls around her are expected to be quiet; she is not, and the film declines to turn that into a lesson.

Two and a half hours is a long stretch for a story that fits in a sentence: a flight attendant, a bag of somebody else's money, and everyone who intends to have it. The extra time goes on people — the phone calls, the drives, the conversations repeated because someone was not listening the first time. Jackie has a job rather than a crew, and the job is what put her within reach of a gunrunner's cash; the police read that as leverage, and they are not entirely wrong. Quentin Tarantino films the scheme as clerical work, which is what schemes are. The bail bondsman she pulls in is the closest thing to an ally she gets, and the film is more interested in what two tired adults say to each other in an ordinary room than in the crime that put them there.

The most valuable object here is a stack of sales leads, kept in a drawer by the front office until the men below prove they deserve them. Premiere Properties is a real estate operation in a bad month. Levene and Moss have years behind them; Roma has the only streak going, and the difference between those two conditions is being converted into a ranking with teeth. A hundred minutes, and James Foley spends nearly all of it on talk — pitches, threats, small extortions conducted in the voice of a favour — because the talk is both the work and the weapon. Then the leads are stolen and the picture turns into a matter of who. Underneath that is something plainer: what men do when their employment is restated as a contest, and the prize is the equipment they need in order to work at all.

The man on trial is the least interesting person in the room, and the film knows it. Bertram Cates taught his students Darwin and was arrested for it; what turns up afterward is a national press corps, a prosecutor who once ran for president and still preaches, and a defence attorney, an old adversary of his, who believes in no god at all. Stanley Kramer keeps everything in the heat — the town, the reporters, the two of them performing for a jury and for the newspapers at once. It runs two hours and eight minutes, most of that cross-examination, with black-and-white photography doing what it can with sweat and crowded rooms. Made in 1960, the film plainly regards the question as still open, which is the part that has not aged.

Cuba under Castro had a use for its artists and a category for its homosexuals, and Reinaldo Arenas was both. Julian Schnabel's film moves across decades in the life of the poet and novelist, and its subject is less a career than a practical problem: how to go on producing sentences in a place where possessing them counts as evidence. That gives the biography an odd centre of gravity. The danger is not one catastrophe but a long administrative pressure applied by people doing their jobs, and 134 minutes leaves room for the ordinary stretches in between, which is where the loss actually registers. Venice's Grand Jury Prize is on its record, and the Academy took note of the lead performance, a part that consists largely of being watched.

An estranged son turns up, which is inconvenient for a man who has spent decades keeping his obligations at arm's length. He is near retirement, pressing a workers' compensation claim, and quietly working for the man he most enjoys annoying — while flirting with that man's young wife, mostly for the sport of it. Robert Benton keeps the scale domestic and the stakes local: a job, a claim, a bank that would like the house he lives in. The comedy comes from repetition rather than incident, from people who have known each other far too long to be surprised. What the film is actually asking is whether a man that far along can still be talked into taking something on. It gives the question 110 minutes and applies no pressure at all.

Nothing in a cell is supposed to change, and that is the problem the film sets for itself. Robert Stroud kills a guard and is put in solitary for the rest of his life; what follows is not escape or revolt but a sparrow found in the exercise yard and kept alive. Out of that comes an education — a man with a third-grade schooling working his way into ornithology, on paper, from inside. John Frankenheimer takes 147 minutes and refuses nearly every incident a prison picture would ordinarily supply. Instead there are guards who come and go, the paperwork, a life accumulating at the scale of one table. The interest lies in what an institution does when a prisoner becomes useful in a way it never intended, and in what freedom can mean when the door is not part of the discussion.

Lenny Bruce's material was held to be too obscene for the public, which leaves a film about him with a blunt difficulty: it has to say the things he was condemned for saying. That is the test this one accepts. Bob Fosse made it in 1975, near enough to the sixties that the fight had not yet become history, and the establishment being described was still partly the one in the seats. The record carries an Academy honour for Best Actress alongside the one for Best Actor, a fair signal that the marriage is not a subplot here; the cost of a life made out of provocation is paid by more than one person. 112 minutes, and everything rests on a hard condition — the routines have to be funny now, in a room where nobody is scandalised.

Mississippi in the summer, a town that runs on one family's money, and a stranger walking in with an accusation of barn-burning behind him. Ben Quick has nerve and very little else, and nerve turns out to be convertible: before long he is inside the Varner house, useful to its head in ways that unsettle everyone else under that roof. Martin Ritt films the South of 1958 as a place where property, marriage and reputation are one transaction conducted in three vocabularies. The heat is not atmosphere but a device, shortening tempers and lengthening evenings. What holds 115 minutes together is the pleasure of watching people who talk well try to get something out of each other without ever admitting that is what they are doing.
